# The Heat Is Urban: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

When a heat wave strikes, the temperature a person actually experiences depends enormously on where, exactly, they are standing. Two neighborhoods in the same city, on the same afternoon, can differ by ten degrees Fahrenheit or more. A treeless parking lot surrounded by asphalt might register 105 degrees, while a shaded street a mile away sits at a comfortable 92. This difference is not an accident of geography—it is the product of design choices, and it means that heat is not merely a weather problem. It is an urban planning problem, and cities have more tools to address it than most people realize. The question is whether they will use them, and how they will navigate the genuine tradeoffs involved.

## The Urban Heat Island

The core problem is what climatologists call the urban heat island effect. Cities replace vegetation and soil with asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops—materials that absorb sunlight during the day and release stored heat slowly through the night. Buildings block the breeze. Cars and air conditioners pump out waste heat.
